title: Value that justifies a price, and respect for where a practice comes from
audience: Yoga, Pilates and personal or group fitness teachers who want to charge more for a class or program and who teach practices with religious or cultural roots.
learningOutcomes: Explain why a higher price needs a benefit the client can see and experience, not a label alone
Write a value statement for a class or program that names the audience, a checkable change, the method and the deliverable, without health or treatment claims
Make and record a decision on how a practice's origins are named, credited and described, and state where the matter is contested

instruction.heading: A higher price needs a benefit the client can feel
instruction.body: Clients pay more when they can see what they are getting. A brand name on its own rarely does that work. A teacher who wants to charge above the local average needs a value that shows up in the room: a small group that allows individual feedback, a clear progression across weeks, a written home plan, a booking system that works, or a cool-down that follows a demanding session. Ask what a client will notice after the third session that they would not notice at a cheaper class. If the answer is only the name, the price rests on the name alone, and that is fragile. Build the premium on something the class delivers and the client can describe in their own words.

instruction.heading: Writing a value statement with a checkable outcome
instruction.body: A value statement connects four things: who the class is for, what changes for them, how the method produces that change, and what they receive. Keep it specific enough to check. A statement such as 'a six-week beginner block for adults returning to exercise, with a written home plan and a progress check at week three' can be verified against the program. A statement that promises to transform a body or cure back pain cannot be verified, and it makes a health claim. Avoid outcome promises about health, injury or weight. Describe what the class does and what the client does in it.

instruction.heading: Respecting where a practice comes from
instruction.body: Some practices, including many forms of yoga, come from traditions that are religious or cultural for some people. Teachers and communities disagree about how such practices should be sold. Some argue that a spiritual practice should not be commercialised. Others argue that teaching it widely and well is a valid way to share it. This lesson does not settle that debate, and it claims no legal rule. As a business owner, you can still take practical steps. Name the source of a practice accurately. Do not imply a lineage, a credential or a religious endorsement that you do not hold. Do not use sacred terms as decoration, and do not describe a practice in a way that mocks its origins. Write down your own position on attribution, so that you can explain it to a client who asks and so that your staff give the same answer.

instruction.heading: Making the same value visible in every channel
instruction.body: The value you describe must match what happens in the room. Put the value statement on the website, the timetable and the bio, and check it against the class plan each term. When a claim changes, change it everywhere on the same day. Use the business name held as {{business:business.display_name}} on every channel so that clients can find one consistent offer. Then ask a small group of current clients to tell you, in their own words, what they pay for. If their answer differs from your value statement, that gap is the next job to fix. Where a class plan relies on a particular safety or evidence standard, keep the reference recorded under {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

procedure: Write four short sentences: the audience, the change for them, the method, and what they receive
Check each sentence against the class plan, and attach a record that shows the element is delivered
Remove any health, treatment or outcome promise that cannot be checked, and leave out any legal point until it is checked.
Write your position on how the practice's origins are named and credited
Put the statement on each channel, and set a review date
Ask three current clients to describe the value in their own words, and record any difference
Adjust the statement or the class, and record which one you changed and why

workedExamples.situation: A fictional teacher, Theo, runs a Pilates studio in Newcastle. He wants to raise the price of a new class and has named it 'The Ancient Method, a cure for back pain'.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should Theo change before he raises the price?
workedExamples.reasoning: Theo should remove the cure claim, because it is an outcome promise he cannot check and it may be regulated. The word 'ancient' is a historical claim that he should use only if he can name and evidence its source. He should describe the class plainly: who it is for, the group size, the progression, the written plan and the feedback the client receives. The higher price then rests on something the client gets, and he should record the change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A fictional yoga teacher, Leilani, is asked by a friend to use a sacred term from a tradition she has studied only briefly, as a catchy name for her Sunday class.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should she decide about the class name?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should not use the sacred term as a marketing name. Using it for decoration misrepresents how much she has studied, and it may offend people for whom the term matters. She can describe the class plainly, name any source she has actually studied, and say what she has studied and for how long. She should write down her position on attribution and share it with her staff.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is required for this lesson
The current class plan for the offer being priced
A draft value statement and a claim review record
A client feedback record, kept with the date of each conversation

commonErrors.error: Pricing on a brand name and a feeling, with no visible benefit in the class
commonErrors.prevention: Name the benefit the client receives in the third session, and check it against the class plan.

commonErrors.error: Writing a health or cure promise into a value statement
commonErrors.prevention: Describe what the class does and what the client does in it. Keep health claims out until they have been checked.

commonErrors.error: Using sacred or tradition terms as decoration
commonErrors.prevention: Use a source name only when you can state what you have studied and how the class relates to it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Health, injury, weight and treatment claims can be regulated in Australia. Do not publish outcome promises about health until they have been checked.
Views on the commercial use of religious or cultural practices differ, and this lesson does not decide them. No legal rule is claimed here.

qualityStandard: The value statement names an audience, a checkable change, a method and a deliverable
No health, cure or treatment claim appears on any channel
The position on attribution is written, dated and shared with staff
documentationEvidence: Value statement, with the date and the class plan reference
Claim review record listing the removed claims and the legal points left out until checked
Client feedback record and any change made as a result
Written attribution position, with the date
summary: A premium needs a benefit the client experiences, not only a name
Write a value statement with a checkable outcome and no health promise
Practices with religious or cultural roots need accurate naming, and your position should be written down
Keep the same value on every channel, and review it with clients

knowledgeChecks.question: A teacher wants to justify a higher price. Which basis is strongest?
options: A visible benefit the client receives in the class, such as a small group and a written progression plan
A brand name the client has seen used in an advert elsewhere and the name of the designer behind it
A claim that the class is better than every other class in the area and the price is the highest locally

knowledgeChecks.question: Which value statement is most appropriate for a publicly listed class?
options: This class cures back pain in six weeks and it is guaranteed for every client who attends each session
A six-week beginner block for adults returning to exercise, with a written home plan and a progress check at week three
Transform your life and your body with the ancient method that has been used for a thousand years by masters

knowledgeChecks.question: A teacher wants to describe a class as part of a religious tradition, but has studied the practice only briefly. What is the appropriate step?
options: Use the tradition's name as the class title to attract more clients and to sell more places each week
Avoid writing down a position, because the matter is contested and leave the teacher to answer questions in class
Describe what has actually been studied, and do not imply a lineage or endorsement that is not held
